claims.text: Enhanced dynamic recovery during deformation is the main cause of the relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has high stacking-fault energy.
High stacking-fault energy and a uniform solid-solution state facilitate rapid dislocation cross-slip and annihilation.
Rapid dislocation cross-slip and annihilation prevent the dislocation accumulation needed for substantial work hardening.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can form a single-phase FCC solid solution.
The equimolar CoCrFeNiTi starting material has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
The undeformed starting material has a low pre-existing dislocation density.
At room temperature, dynamic recovery is active in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Cryogenic deformation suppresses dynamic recovery relative to room-temperature deformation.
Room-temperature cross-slip and recovery limit dislocation pile-up and net dislocation density.
Lower net dislocation density produces a reduced work-hardening rate.
The proposed recovery mechanism explains the combination of favorable ductility and machinability with relatively low hardness and strength.
Room-temperature deformation will produce limited dislocation accumulation, a low strain-hardening rate, and only modest hardness increases.
Cryogenic deformation will produce a higher dislocation density than room-temperature deformation.
Cryogenic deformation will produce greater work hardening than room-temperature deformation.
Cryogenically deformed samples will have higher post-deformation hardness than room-temperature-deformed samples.
The mechanism applies at strain rates around 10^-3 s^-1 when the alloy remains single-phase FCC over room-temperature to cryogenic loading.
Failure to observe significantly higher dislocation density, strain hardening, and hardness under cryogenic loading would falsify the dynamic-recovery hypothesis.
